newsitem.title: USA: Caution needed on E-money regulation - U.S. official.
newsitem.headline: Caution needed on E-money regulation - U.S. official.

text.p: Government regulators should carefully monitor new developments in the use of electronic money but they should avoid taking sweeping action before the industry has time to evolve, an official with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) said Tuesday.
"In my view, patience is key," said James Kamihachi, senior deputy comptroller for economic and policy analysis at the OCC.
Kamihachi told the National Economists Club that premature regulation could have a "chilling effect" on development of new technology.

"It's important to allow many of the issues to be resolved in the private sector," he said, adding that when government intervention is needed, it should be applied with a "scalpel rather than a meat ax."
Kamihachi said that his remarks were his own opinions and did not necessarily reflect those of the OCC, the Comptroller or the U.S. Treasury.
However, U.S. Comptroller Eugene Ludwig has also cautioned against premature regulation of electronic money.

In his speech, Kamihachi pointed to financial incentives that could boost the use of electronic money transactions, such as the fact that processing a single check costs $1 while an electronic transaction only costs a few cents.
On the other hand, heavy reliance among U.S. consumers on credit cards might make electronic money a "tough sell" in the United States, he said.

The OCC official listed a number of areas where the government might need to become involved, including helping to determine who may be liable when a transaction fails and taking action against fraud and counterfeiting.
The issue of geography is among the complications that could arise as electronic transactions over the Internet increase.
"Most banking laws are rooted in some notion of geography," he noted. The notion could become moot if money transactions over the Internet become highly prevalent, he said.
